Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Enforcing the law and maintaining public order
Situation2: A public protest begins to escalate, with tension rising between opposing groups
Story:
My phone buzzed just as I was about to step out of the precinct. It was Jamie, my oldest friend, his name flashing with a video call request. “Hey, can you help me? These instructions make no sense and I’m about to lose it,” he texted, sounding desperate. I knew he’d just moved in and was struggling to get his new place set up. As his friend, I wanted to be there, to offer a few minutes of calm and guidance, just like he’d done for me so many times before.

But as I glanced at the screen, my radio crackled to life. Reports of a protest downtown were coming in—crowds gathering, voices rising, the situation teetering on the edge. As a police officer, I was expected to respond immediately, to help keep the peace and prevent things from spiraling out of control. My duty was clear, but so was my loyalty to Jamie. I felt the weight of both roles pressing in, each demanding my presence, each expecting me to put them first. My thumb hovered over the phone, heart pounding, torn between the friend who needed me and the badge that called me to serve.
